unit.title: Communicate and interact effectively in the workplace

summary: This unit teaches the communication skills a beauty therapist uses every day: greeting clients, carrying out a consultation, listening and questioning, speaking in plain words, reading body language, and respecting differences between people. You will also learn to take bookings and write short messages, keep client information private, work well with co-workers, deal with complaints and disagreements, and take part in meetings and feedback.

blocks.p: Beauty therapy is a people business. A client can forgive a slightly uneven nail shape, but she will not forgive being ignored, rushed or talked about. This unit is about how you speak, listen, write and behave with clients and with the people you work with. It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees, and every other unit in the programme depends on it: you cannot do a safe facial, wax or manicure until you have found out, through good communication, what the client wants and whether the treatment is safe for her.

Good communication does three jobs in a salon or spa. It keeps clients **safe** (you find out about allergies, health and medicines). It gives clients the **service they want** (you check, you do not guess). And it keeps the **team working well** (everyone knows the bookings, the jobs and the problems).

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the salon
rows: Communicate clearly and politely with clients
Greet clients warmly and use a clear, friendly voice
Use plain words, not trade jargon
Show care through your body language and tone
Carry out a consultation
Use open and closed questions
Listen actively and check that you understand
Record answers, explain the plan and get the client's agreement
Talk with clients during treatment
Check her comfort without disturbing her
Respect her wish for quiet or for conversation
Explain aftercare simply, and in writing
Respect differences between people
Treat every client fairly and with dignity
Adapt for clients with a disability, a language barrier or a cultural or religious need
Handle bookings, calls and messages
Book appointments accurately
Write short, polite messages
Use the telephone and phone messaging professionally
Keep information confidential
Keep records safe and private
Share client details only with people who need them, or with the client's permission
Work well with co-workers
Hand over clearly
Support and welcome others
Keep personal matters out of the treatment area
Deal with complaints and disagreements
Listen calmly and apologise where right
Agree and record what will be done
Sort out disagreements politely and in private
Take part in meetings and give and receive feedback
Prepare, listen, speak briefly and follow up
Accept feedback and give it kindly and specifically

flow: Greet the client
Consult and agree the plan
Give the treatment while checking comfort
Give aftercare advice
Take payment and book the next visit
Record and hand over
Follow up if needed

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon or spa: consultations and booking by role play, then handling a complaint and holding a team meeting. The assessor watches how you greet, listen, question, explain, record and behave, not only what you say.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In role plays, photograph only cards, papers, hands and backs. Do not photograph a member's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Communication happens when one person sends a message and the other person receives it and understands it the way it was meant. If the message is not understood, communication has not happened, however much was said.

flow: The sender has an idea or need
She puts it into words, a look or a sign
The message travels (speech, writing, phone, gesture)
The receiver hears or sees it
The receiver works out its meaning
The receiver answers: this is feedback
The sender checks it was understood

head: Kind
What it is
Examples in a salon
rows: Verbal
Messages in spoken or written words.
Greeting a client, asking about her skin, a booking text, a price list, a consent form.
Non-verbal
Messages without words: **body language**, facial expression, posture, gestures, eye contact, distance and **tone of voice**.
A smile at reception, folded arms, looking at your phone while she talks, a gentle touch on the shoulder with her permission.

blocks.p: Clients notice how you say something as much as what you say. When your words and your body language disagree, the client believes your body language. If you say 'I'm happy to help' with a sigh and a glance at the clock, she hears 'I'm busy'.

ul: **Tone** is the warmth, sharpness or friendliness people hear in your voice. A calm, warm tone relaxes a client. A sharp or bored tone makes her feel unwelcome.
**Pace**: speak at a steady speed. Too fast, and she cannot follow. Too slow, and she feels talked down to.
**Volume**: loud enough to be heard over music and dryers, but never shouting. In a treatment room, keep your voice soft so that you do not disturb other clients.
**Words**: choose polite, simple words. Avoid nicknames such as 'darling' or 'sweetie' unless the Centre or the salon allows it and the client likes it. Never use slang that could offend.

head: Good body language
Poor body language
rows: Smile; friendly eye contact (not staring)
Looking away, rolling eyes, yawning
Open posture: relaxed shoulders, hands visible
Folded arms, leaning away, hands in pockets
Facing the client when she speaks
Turning your back or looking at a screen or phone
Nodding to show you are following
Tapping a foot or checking the time
Standing or sitting at her eye level for a consultation
Standing over her while she is seated

blocks.note: Eye contact and touch have different meanings in different cultures and for different people. Some clients feel uncomfortable with long eye contact or with touch. Watch her reaction and adjust. Always tell a client before you touch her and why.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A client forms an opinion of you and of the salon in the first few seconds. That **first impression** comes from your appearance, your smile, your greeting, and how the reception area looks and smells. A clean uniform, tied-back hair, clean hands and nails, and a welcoming greeting all say 'you are in safe hands'.

ul: Stop what you are doing, look up, smile and greet her within a few moments. If you are on the phone, smile and nod to show that you have seen her.
Use her name once you know it, and say yours. In Jamaica, use Miss, Mrs, Mr or the title she prefers until she invites you to use her first name.
Offer a seat and tell her how long she will wait. Do not leave her standing without a word.

head: Barrier
Example
How to overcome it
rows: Noise
Dryers, loud music, a crowded salon
Move to a quieter area
Turn the music down
Face the client and speak clearly
Language
A visitor who speaks little English; heavy patois or fast speech
Use simple words and short sentences
Use pictures, a price list, gestures or a written note
Ask a colleague who speaks her language to help
Jargon
'Exfoliate', 'comedones', 'hypertrophic'
Use plain words: 'remove dead skin', 'blackheads', 'raised scar'.
Distraction
Phone, other clients, tiredness
Give the client your full attention; put your phone away.
Feelings
A nervous client, an angry client, a stressed therapist
Stay calm, speak slowly, show you understand, and take a short pause if you need it.
Hearing or sight loss
A client who is hard of hearing or who cannot see well
Face her, speak clearly, write if needed, describe what you are doing.
Assuming
Thinking you know what she means
Check by repeating it back in your own words.

blocks.p: The **consultation** is the conversation before a treatment. You find out what the client wants, check that the treatment is safe for her, agree a plan, explain it, and record it. It is the most important communication task in the unit, because a skipped consultation is how burns, allergic reactions and unhappy clients happen.

flow: Greet the client by name and take her to a private area
Explain why you are asking questions
Ask open questions about her needs
Ask closed questions to check facts and safety
Listen actively and write down the answers
Look at the skin, nails or area to be treated and check for contra-indications
Explain the treatment, products, time and price in plain words
Sum up and check she agrees
Get her signature on the consent form, then begin

head: Type
What it is
Examples
Use it to
rows: Open question
Cannot be answered with just 'yes' or 'no'. Often begins with what, how, why, when or 'tell me'.
'How does your skin feel by the end of the day?'
'What would you like from today's facial?'
'Tell me about the last time you had your legs waxed.'
Get the client talking; find out her needs, feelings and routine.
Closed question
Can be answered with 'yes', 'no' or one fact.
'Are you allergic to anything?'
'Are you pregnant?'
'Are you taking any medicine for your skin?'
Check facts, safety and contra-indications; confirm what was said.
Probing question
A follow-up that asks for more detail.
'What happened after you used that cream?'
'Can you tell me more about that?'
Dig deeper when an answer is short or unclear.
Leading question
Suggests the answer you want.
'You do want the expensive package, don't you?'
Avoid it. It pushes the client and spoils trust.

blocks.p: Start with open questions and move to closed questions for the safety checks. If you start with a closed question, such as 'Do you have oily skin?', you may only get 'Yes' and learn very little.
**Active listening** means giving the speaker your full attention and showing that you have understood. It is more than staying quiet.

ul: Face the client, look at her, and put down your pen or phone when she is speaking about something important.
Nod and use small sounds ('I see', 'mm-hm') to show you are following.
Do not interrupt or finish her sentences.
Ask a question when something is unclear.
**Paraphrase**: say it back in your own words. 'So your skin feels tight after cleansing and you want something to calm the redness. Is that right?'
Watch her face and body as well as listening to her words. A client who says 'it's fine' with a tight face may not be fine.

**Sum up** the plan before you start: what you will do, with which products, how long it will take and how much it costs in J$. This checks that you and the client agree and that she is not surprised later.
Ask 'Do you have any questions?' and answer honestly. If you do not know, say so and find out; never make up an answer.

A **consent form** is the record that the client agrees to the treatment after it was explained. She signs it before you start. A client who is unsure, or who says no, must not be pressed. If a client is under 18, follow the Centre's policy: a parent or guardian usually gives the consent.

blocks.note: If your consultation shows a contra-indication, such as infected skin, a recent injury, a possible allergic reaction or a serious health condition, do not give the treatment. Tell the client calmly and privately, in plain words. Do not name the disease. Suggest that she sees her doctor, and offer to rebook when she is better. Write it on the record card.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Always carry out a patch test when the treatment or product requires it, and explain to the client why: it is a small test on the skin to check for a reaction before the full treatment.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Talking with clients during and after treatment

ul: Check comfort at the start of a treatment and from time to time: 'Is the pressure all right?' 'Is the wax too warm?' Use a quiet voice.
Watch for signs she is uncomfortable: tensing, flinching, holding her breath, frowning, shifting on the couch. Ask, adjust, and do not wait for a complaint.
A client who is silent is not always happy. Ask a simple question: 'Is this pressure good for you?'
Never keep going until the client complains, and never assume that no reply means everything is fine.

blocks.p: Some clients want to chat; others want to rest. Let the client lead.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Offer a quiet treatment and watch for her response
Talk on and on about your own life or problems
Keep conversation light, positive and about her interests
Discuss other clients or gossip about co-workers
Keep conversation about the treatment simple
Argue about politics, religion or money
Stay quiet when she closes her eyes and relaxes
Use the treatment to sell her products she does not need

blocks.p: Use words the client knows. **Jargon** is trade language that clients may not understand. If you must use a technical word, explain it.

head: Jargon
Plain words
rows: Exfoliate
Gently remove dead skin cells
Contra-indication
A reason why we cannot do this treatment today
Patch test
A small test on your skin to see if you react
Occlusive
A layer that seals moisture in
Erythema
Redness of the skin

ul: Give advice **in words and in writing**: a short aftercare sheet. Clients forget much of what they hear, especially when relaxed.
Say what to do, what not to do, how long, and when to call the salon. For example, after a wax: no hot baths, sun or tight clothes for 24 hours; no scrubbing; call us if the skin blisters.
Ask her to repeat the main points. If she cannot, explain again in simpler words and show her. Do not repeat the same words more loudly.
Check she understands any home-care products and how to use them. Be honest: do not claim a product will do more than it can.

blocks.p: Offering a product or another service is part of the job, but the client's needs come first. Recommend what suits her skin and budget. Never pressure her, never say a product will cure a medical problem, and accept 'no' politely.

blocks.h: When you do not know the answer

blocks.p: Clients ask about medicines, medical conditions, pregnancy, and treatments you have not been trained to give. Say honestly that you do not know or that it is outside your training, and suggest she asks her doctor or pharmacist. Never guess, and never give medical advice.

Clients and co-workers differ in culture, age, religion, language, gender, ability, health and background. **Diversity** means these differences. A professional treats everyone fairly, politely and with dignity, and does not judge, joke about, stare at or avoid anyone because they are different from her.

head: Client
What you can do
rows: A client with a hearing difficulty
Face her, with light on your face, so she can see your lips
Speak clearly at a normal pace; do not shout
Write notes or use a pad
Use a few signs or gestures; some Deaf people in Jamaica use **Jamaican Sign Language (JSL)**; ask if she would like an interpreter and book one if she does
A client with a sight difficulty
Say who you are and tell her what you are doing before you touch her
Describe the layout of the room and guide her gently if she asks you to
Tell her when you move away
A client who uses a wheelchair or walking frame
Speak to her, not to the person pushing the chair
Ask how she wants to be helped; do not move her or her chair without asking
Check that the treatment area is accessible
A client who speaks little English
Use simple words, short sentences and pictures
Write down prices and times
Be patient; do not speak louder
Ask a colleague who knows her language
An older client
Speak respectfully and do not talk down to her
Allow extra time; check she is warm and comfortable
Be careful with skin, medicines and balance
A client with a religious or cultural need
Ask what she needs; offer privacy, or a therapist of her own sex
Do not tease or ask personal questions out of curiosity
A nervous or first-time client
Explain each step
Show her the products and tools
Let her stop the treatment at any time

blocks.note: If a client asks for a female therapist, a private room, or a different time for a religious or personal reason, arrange it if you can, or offer another time. Do not laugh, argue or call her difficult.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Talk to the client herself, even if she has a friend, a carer, an interpreter or a child with her. Speak to the helper only if the client asks you to. Do not talk about her in front of her as if she is not there.

ul: Treat every client with the same politeness whatever her age, shape, skin colour, income, religion, health or disability.
Do not refuse or rush a client because you are uncomfortable. If there is a real safety reason to refuse (a contra-indication), explain it kindly.

Jamaican law protects people from unfair treatment in several areas, and the Centre has its own rules. Follow the Centre's policy on respect and non-discrimination. Ask your instructor if you are unsure.

blocks.note: Be aware of the words you use for people. Say 'a client who uses a wheelchair', not 'a wheelchair person'. Ask what term she prefers. Do not ask about her condition unless it matters for the treatment.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Greet the caller and give the salon name and your name
Ask what she wants and who it is for
Check the book or system for a free time that suits her
Give the day, date, time, service and price in J$
Take her name and phone number
Repeat everything back to check
Thank her; confirm by message if the salon does this

ul: Write the booking at once, clearly, in the right column. Include the service, the therapist, the length of time, and any special need (for example, a first visit or an allergy).
Allow the right time for each service, including setting up and cleaning. A double-booking leaves one client waiting and the therapist rushing.
If a client wants a time that is not free, offer two or three other times; do not just say 'no'.
If you make a change, such as a cancellation or a new time, update the book or system immediately and tell the therapist.
Remember that the **appointment book** shows everybody who is booked, when and for what, so that the whole team knows how the day will run.
Answer quickly, smile (it is heard in your voice) and speak clearly: 'Good morning, Glow Beauty Studio, this is Marcia. How may I help you?'
Do not eat or chew while on the phone. Keep a pen and the booking book ready.
Take a message when needed: who called, her phone number, the date and time, the message, and who it is for. Read it back to the caller.
If you must put a caller on hold, say why and for how long, and thank her for waiting.
Do not take or make personal calls in front of clients.

blocks.p: Many Jamaican salons confirm bookings and answer questions by text or WhatsApp. These messages represent the salon, so write them as carefully as a letter.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Greet, name the salon and give clear details: day, date, time, service
Use text-speak, slang, ALL CAPITALS or lots of emojis
Be polite and short; check spelling and numbers before you send
Sound rude or threatening, even when a client is often late
Reply within a reasonable time, and update the booking if the client changes it
Ignore a message or remember a change without telling anyone
Use the salon's own number or account for client business
Post a client's photo or details online without her written permission

blocks.p: A good reminder reads: 'Good afternoon Ms Reid. This is a reminder that your facial is booked for Friday 14 March at 2 p.m. with Marcia. Please call us on 876-555-0123 if you need to change it. Thank you.'

ul: A **notice** to staff: short title, date, what is changing, from when, and who to ask.
A **handover note**: what was done, what is left, any concerns, and the time.
Use plain words and short sentences. Check names, dates, times and prices before you hand it over or post it.
Write clearly in ink on records; never remove or cover over an entry with correction fluid. Put one line through a mistake, initial it and write the correction.

blocks.p: Clients tell you private things: health problems, medicines, pregnancy, allergies, skin conditions, her address and phone number. **Confidentiality** means keeping this information private and not sharing it without her permission. Clients trust you only if you keep it.

ul: It protects the client from embarrassment, unfair treatment and harm.
It keeps her trust, so she comes back and tells you the truth next time. Hiding a medical fact can make a treatment unsafe.
It protects the good name of the salon and your job.
Jamaica's data protection law (the Data Protection Act) requires businesses to handle personal information carefully. Follow the Centre's and the salon's policy.

head: Where
What to do
rows: In speech
Talk about clients' health and treatments only in private, never at reception or on the salon floor
Do not tell friends or family who your clients are or what they had done
Never discuss one client with another
On paper
Keep record cards in a closed cabinet, locked when the salon is closed
Do not leave cards on the counter or couch
Shred or burn old cards as the policy says
On computers and phones
Use passwords; lock the screen when you leave
Do not store client details on your own phone or share them in a staff chat
Back up safely
Online
Do not post photos, names or stories about clients on social media without her written permission
Ask her first, even for 'before and after' pictures

blocks.h: When someone asks about a client

blocks.p: If a friend, a family member or a caller asks about a client, say politely that you cannot share any client's details. If the client's husband or mother asks, the same rule applies. Share information only with the client's permission, or with a person who needs it to give safe care: for example, another therapist who is taking over the treatment, or a doctor when the client asks you to. In an emergency, give the ambulance crew what they need.

blocks.note: Staff must also keep the salon's own business private: prices not yet announced, staff problems and takings. Never complain about the salon or its clients on social media.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A **record card** holds the client's details, her consultation answers, any contra-indications, patch-test results, the treatment given (with products, strengths and timings), aftercare advice and her signed consent.
Fill it in clearly, truthfully and at the time. Sign and date it.
Why? So that any therapist can see what was done and work safely; so you can compare progress; and so there is proof if a complaint or a reaction happens.
The record card belongs to the salon but the information belongs to the client. Let her see her own card if she asks.

blocks.p: A salon team works well when everyone knows their role, the day's plan and the standards expected, and when people help each other. Clients notice a team that works well, and one that does not.

ul: A **briefing** (or huddle) is a short meeting at the start of the day: the bookings, special clients, absences, stock problems and any news. Arrive on time with a pen.

A **handover** is what you tell a co-worker who takes over from you, at a break or at the end of a shift: what was done, what is left, and any concerns about a client. Be clear and complete. Giving a poor handover can mean a client is missed, hurt or double-charged.
Keep a **communication book** or noticeboard for messages, and check it each day.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Be on time, and tell your supervisor early if you will be late
Leave a colleague to cover for you without warning
Offer to help when you finish early: prepare the next room, restock, fold towels
Sit in the staff room while others are rushed
Ask when you are unsure
Guess and hope that nobody notices
Share tools and the work fairly
Take the best jobs, or leave jobs for others
Be polite and keep personal matters private in front of clients
Use private jokes, nicknames or arguments in front of clients
Welcome a new member: introduce her, show her around, offer help
Leave her alone, give her the worst jobs, or gossip about her

blocks.p: If your supervisor or two co-workers each give you a job and you cannot do both at once, **tell them** and ask which comes first. Do not silently do the easy job or rush all of them. Clients, safety and hygiene come before tidying or restocking.

blocks.note: Messages from co-workers can get changed as they pass from person to person. For anything important, such as a change to a client's booking or a safety issue, speak to the person directly or write it down.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A complaint is a chance to put things right and keep the client. Most clients who feel listened to stay loyal. Never take a complaint personally.

flow: Stay calm and take her somewhere private
Listen to all of it without interrupting
Show you understand and apologise for how she feels
Ask questions and look at the problem (the skin, the nails, the bill)
Agree what will be done, following the salon's policy
Do it, or pass it to the manager quickly
Write it on the complaint record
Follow up later, and use it to improve

ul: **Do not** argue, blame a co-worker, make excuses, or tell the client she is wrong.
**Do not** promise something you cannot give, such as a full refund, if the policy does not allow it. Say what you can do, and who can decide the rest.
If she is angry and shouting, stay calm, lower your voice and speak slowly. Offer to talk in private. If you feel unsafe, get your supervisor.
If she has a skin reaction or an injury, treat it as a health matter first: look after her, give first aid if trained, advise her to see a doctor, and report it at once.

blocks.p: **Why record it?** A written record shows what happened, what was agreed, and who will act. The manager can then find patterns (for example, the same therapist or the same product) and improve the service.
Conflict is a disagreement between people that needs to be sorted out. It happens in every workplace. It is how you handle it that counts.

head: Style
What it sounds like
Result
rows: Aggressive
'You are so lazy! You never clean up!'
The other person defends herself; it gets worse.
Passive
Says nothing, complains behind her back, resents the other person
The problem stays and the mood sours.
Assertive
'I feel stressed when the trolley is not restocked. Can we agree who does it?'
Calm, respectful, and the problem gets solved.

blocks.p: **Assertive** means standing up for yourself calmly and respectfully, without being rude or aggressive.

flow: Calm down first; do not speak in anger
Choose a private place and a quiet time, never in front of clients
Describe the problem, not the person, with an 'I' statement
Listen to her side
Agree a solution together
Thank her and check it again later
If it does not work, take it to your supervisor

blocks.note: Do not complain about a co-worker to clients, post about it on social media, or stop speaking to her for days. Go to your supervisor when talking calmly has not solved it, or earlier if it involves harassment, bullying or safety.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Taking part in a staff meeting

head: When
What you do
rows: Before
Read the agenda (the list of items)
Think about what you want to say and bring any facts
Arrive on time with a pen and paper; silence your phone
During
Listen without interrupting; wait your turn
Keep your points short and to the item being discussed
Speak up when you have a good idea; do not stay silent if you have something useful to offer
Disagree politely: 'I see it differently because...'
After
Read the minutes and check they are correct
Do the tasks you agreed, by the date
Tell the chairperson if you cannot

head: Role
Job
rows: Chairperson
Opens and closes the meeting, follows the agenda, makes sure everyone can speak, and keeps order.
Minute-taker
Writes down what is said and agreed: the decisions and the actions.
Timekeeper
Watches the clock so that each item has its time.
Member
Listens, contributes and carries out her actions.

blocks.p: **Minutes** are the short written record of a meeting: the date, who came, what was decided and what must be done. An **action plan** lists the tasks agreed, who will do each one, and by when. Send the minutes out soon after the meeting.
**Feedback** is information about how someone did something, given to help her improve. Both giving and receiving it are professional skills.

head: Giving feedback
Receiving feedback
rows: Choose a good time and a private place
Listen without interrupting or arguing
Start with something specific that went well
Do not take it personally; it is about the work
Name one or two things to improve, with examples about the work, not the person
Ask questions if you are not sure what she means
Say how to improve: 'Hold the skin tighter next time'
Thank her, even if it is hard to hear
End with encouragement and check she understands
Decide what you will change and do it

ul: Compare: 'Good, even shape. Next time hold the skin tighter.' (helpful: specific and kind) with 'It was fine, I suppose.' (vague) and 'That was terrible.' (harsh and unhelpful).
Clients give feedback too. A short feedback form or a friendly 'How was your treatment?' helps the salon improve. Record it and share it with the team.
I can explain why good communication keeps clients safe, satisfied and the team working well.
I can tell the difference between verbal and non-verbal communication, and give examples of good and poor body language.
I can explain how tone, pace and word choice affect a client.
I can greet a client well and say why first impressions matter.
I can name common barriers to communication and say how to overcome each.
I can carry out a consultation in the right order and say what each step is for.
I can tell open, closed, probing and leading questions apart and use them correctly.
I can listen actively and paraphrase to check I understand.
I can sum up a plan, explain a treatment in plain words and get a signed consent form.
I can handle a contra-indication kindly, in private, and refer the client to her doctor.
I can check a client's comfort during treatment, and give aftercare advice in words and in writing.
I can adapt how I communicate for clients with hearing, sight or mobility needs, little English, or cultural or religious needs.
I can take a booking, a phone message and write a polite confirmation message.
I can say why client information is confidential, and how to protect it in speech, on paper, on computers and online.
I can fill in a client record card accurately.
I can hand over to a co-worker, support a newcomer and ask what comes first when I am busy.
I can deal with a complaint calmly and record it.
I can sort out a disagreement assertively and in private.
I can take part well in a meeting, and give and receive feedback.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. Example: 'I take the client to a private area so that she can speak freely about her health.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Verbal communication
Messages in spoken or written words.
Non-verbal communication
Messages without words: body language, facial expression, gestures and tone of voice.
Body language
What your face, posture and movements say to other people.
Tone of voice
The warmth, sharpness or friendliness people hear in your voice.
First impression
The opinion someone forms of you in the first few seconds.
Feedback
The reply or information that shows whether a message was understood, or how someone did a task.
Barrier
Anything that stops a message being received or understood.
Consultation
The private conversation before a treatment to find the client's needs and check safety.
Open question
A question that cannot be answered with just yes or no.
Closed question
A question that can be answered with yes, no or one fact.
Active listening
Listening with full attention, showing interest and checking that you understand.
Paraphrase
Saying what someone said in your own words, to check you understood.
Jargon
Words used only by people in one trade, which clients may not understand.
Contra-indication
A reason why a treatment must not be given, or must be changed.
Consent form
The form a client signs to show she agrees to a treatment after it has been explained.
Patch test
A small test on the skin to check for a reaction before a treatment.
Diversity
The differences between people: culture, age, religion, ability, language and background.
Jamaican Sign Language (JSL)
The language of signs used by many Deaf people in Jamaica.
Confidentiality
Keeping a client's information private and not sharing it without her permission.
Record card
The client's record of her details, consultation, treatment, advice and consent.
Briefing
A short meeting at the start of the day to go over bookings and problems.
Handover
Passing a client or a job to a co-worker, with what was done and what is left.
Conflict
A disagreement between people at work that needs to be sorted out.
Assertive
Standing up for yourself calmly and respectfully, without being rude or aggressive.
Complaint record
A written note of a complaint, what was agreed and who will act.
Agenda
The list of items to be discussed at a meeting.
Chairperson
The person who runs a meeting.
Minutes
The written record of what was said and decided at a meeting.
Action plan
A list of agreed tasks, with who will do each one and by when.

c1.title: A bride's first facial in Mandeville
c1.text: Shanice Brown, 24, is getting married in three weeks and has booked her first facial at a spa in Mandeville. Therapist Kemoy greets her at reception, takes her to a quiet treatment room and starts the consultation. Shanice says she is nervous, that her skin 'breaks out', and that she wants it clear for the wedding. Kemoy needs to learn about her skin, her products, any allergies and her health, and to explain the treatment and price of J$6,500.

c2.title: A visitor at the hotel spa in Negril
c2.text: Mrs Anke Weber, a visitor from Germany, comes to the spa at a hotel in Negril for a manicure. She speaks only a little English. Therapist Latoya is tired at the end of a long day, and the spa's speakers are playing loud music. Mrs Weber points to a photo of nail art on the wall and asks 'How long? How much?'

c3.title: An older client with a walking frame in Spanish Town
c3.text: Miss Ivy Rowe, 72, uses a walking frame and comes with her daughter Pauline to a salon in Spanish Town for a pedicure. Miss Rowe is hard of hearing in her left ear. Trainee Racquel is unsure how to speak to her. Pauline answers all the questions for her mother. During the foot massage, Miss Rowe suddenly goes quiet and her shoulders tense.

c4.title: A complaint about a wax in Portmore
c4.text: Mrs Donna Grant returns to a salon in Portmore the day after a leg wax. Her legs are red and sore, and she says the wax was far too hot. Therapist Odane, who gave the wax, is at the salon but is busy with another client. Trainee Shelly is at reception and the salon is full of people waiting.

c5.title: Gossip and a missed handover in Ocho Rios
c5.text: At a salon in Ocho Rios, therapist Alecia finishes at 1 p.m. and hands her client, Mrs Hall, over to therapist Brian to finish a half-done paraffin hand treatment. Alecia says only 'She's all yours.' Later Brian tells a friend in the staff room, in front of a visitor, that Mrs Hall mentioned she is pregnant. Another member of staff, Tasha, often leaves the shared nail desk untidy, and Brian is getting angry about it.

c6.title: The staff meeting at a spa in Savanna-la-Mar
c6.text: The owner of a small spa in Savanna-la-Mar, Mrs Lyn, holds a 20-minute staff meeting on Monday at 8:30 a.m. The agenda has three items: the new booking system, the towel laundry and the holiday rota. Junior therapist Kerry-Ann has an idea about confirming bookings by WhatsApp. Nadine is chosen as the minute-taker, and Mrs Lyn is the chairperson.

questions.q: Kemoy wants to begin Shanice's consultation so that she talks freely about her skin. Which opening question is best?
o: How does your skin behave in the weeks before a big event?
Do you get spots on your chin when you are stressed or tired?
Is your skin oily, dry or a mixture of both on most days?
Have you ever had a facial or a skin treatment before today?
questions.why: An open question needs more than a word to answer, so it draws out how she feels and what she does. The others can be answered with one word or a choice, so they give far less information.

questions.q: Shanice says, 'I use a cream my cousin gave me, and I think it has something strong in it.' What should Kemoy do?
o: Tell her it is probably fine and carry on, since creams from relatives are usually mild
Ask her to bring in the cream and its label next visit, and book the facial then
Ask whether she would rather stop using any creams altogether before the wedding
Ask what it does, what it did to her skin and when she last used it
questions.why: A probing question gets the detail Kemoy needs to judge whether the facial is safe today. Guessing it is fine, or waiting until the next visit, puts the client at risk.

questions.q: Shanice mentions that she takes tablets from her doctor for acne. What should Kemoy do?
o: Ignore it, because tablets taken by mouth cannot affect a facial treatment on the skin
Tell her to stop the tablets for a week before the wedding so that her skin can settle
Record it and follow the salon's policy before treating her
Promise that the facial will help the tablets to work faster on her skin
questions.why: Some acne medicines make the skin more sensitive and may be a contra-indication. Record it and follow the policy or get medical advice. Never tell a client to change her medicine and never promise results.

questions.q: At the end of the consultation, which step shows that Kemoy and Shanice agree on the facial?
o: Kemoy starts gently and asks Shanice to say if she dislikes anything along the way
Kemoy sums up the plan and price, and Shanice signs the consent form
Shanice reads the product labels while Kemoy prepares the room and the trolley
Kemoy writes 'consultation done' on the record card and then begins the facial
questions.why: Summing up checks that both understand the plan, time and cost, and the signed consent form is the record of her agreement. Starting first, or just noting that a consultation took place, does not prove agreement.

questions.q: What is the best way for Latoya to answer Mrs Weber's question 'How long? How much?'
o: Write the time and price on a card and point to the item
Speak louder and faster so that she can catch the words as they go past
Ask the receptionist to deal with it, as she is busy at the end of a long day
Smile and say 'Half an hour, okay?' and leave out the price to save time
questions.why: Writing the details and pointing to the picture uses more than one channel and works round the language barrier. Louder, faster speech does not make words easier to understand.

questions.q: Which action best deals with the loud music?
o: Lean in close and raise your voice to ask the question again and again
Ask Mrs Weber to come back another day when the spa is quieter and calmer
Leave the music on, because it helps guests to relax and she will adjust
Ask for the music to be turned down, or move to a quiet corner
questions.why: Cutting the noise and speaking face to face lets her hear and see the words. Shouting is uncomfortable, and sending her away is poor service.

questions.q: Nadine is the minute-taker. Which of these should her minutes record?
o: Each person's words exactly as spoken, including jokes and side comments
Her own opinion on whether each idea put forward was good or bad
The decisions made and the actions agreed, with names and dates
Only the items on which everyone at the meeting agreed without discussion
questions.why: Minutes are a short record of who came, what was decided and what must be done, with names and dates, so that people can check and act. They are not a word-for-word script or a place for personal opinion.

questions.q: Mrs Weber nods but looks puzzled while Latoya explains the aftercare. What should Latoya do?
o: Take the nod as a yes and move on to the payment and the next booking
Show the steps with pictures or a simple sheet, and ask her to show what she will do
Repeat the same sentence again, more slowly and a little more loudly
Give her the product and tell her to read the label when she gets home
questions.why: A nod does not prove understanding. Showing the steps and asking her to demonstrate checks that the message got through.

questions.q: Pauline keeps answering her mother's questions for her. What should Racquel do?
o: Ask Miss Rowe directly, and involve Pauline only if Miss Rowe asks
Let Pauline carry on answering, since she is the family member who knows her best
Ask Pauline to wait outside for the whole service so that her mother can speak
Write the questions on the card and hand it to Pauline to fill in for her
questions.why: The client herself is the person to speak to, even when a relative is present. A helper joins in only at the client's request.

questions.q: Which approach helps Racquel communicate best with Miss Rowe, who is hard of hearing in one ear?
o: Stand behind her and speak in a normal voice, so that she hears from her better ear
Shout from across the room so that the words carry over the noise of the salon
Speak to the daughter and use hand signals with the mother to save time
Face her in good light, speak clearly and write if needed
questions.why: Many people with hearing loss lip-read and watch your expression. Face her, speak clearly without shouting and add writing. Shouting distorts words and is unkind.

questions.q: During the foot massage Miss Rowe goes quiet and her shoulders tense. What is the best response?
o: Carry on, because silence usually means a client is relaxed and enjoying it
Tell her to relax and keep still so that the massage can be finished on time
Ask quietly if the pressure is comfortable, and adjust it
Finish the massage early without saying anything, to avoid upsetting her
questions.why: Silence and tense muscles can mean discomfort. A quiet question and a change of pressure shows care. Telling her to relax does not deal with the cause.

questions.q: Miss Rowe must move from her walking frame to the pedicure chair. What should Racquel do?
o: Take her arm and lift her into the chair to save time for the next client
Ask Miss Rowe how she would like to be helped
Move the frame out of her reach first so that it is not in the way
Ask Pauline to lift her, as she knows how her mother likes to be moved
questions.why: Clients know best how they move. Ask first, never lift or move her or her frame without permission, and stay close in case she needs support.

questions.q: Mrs Grant arrives upset. What should Shelly do first?
o: Take her somewhere private, listen to all of it and apologise that she is sore
Ask her to wait quietly at the desk until Odane has finished with her client
Tell her that some redness is normal after a wax and will fade in a day or two
Ask her to write the complaint down and come back tomorrow when it is quieter
questions.why: A private place and calm listening show the client she has been heard and keep the complaint away from other clients. Explaining it away or sending her off makes her angrier and ignores a possible injury.

questions.q: Mrs Grant says, 'Odane was careless!' What should Shelly say?
o: That Odane is often careless, and offer her a free wax to make up for it
That Mrs Grant must have a sensitive skin, so it is not Odane's fault at all
That staff should not be blamed while the salon is so busy with clients
That she is sorry, will look at the skin, and the manager will look into it
questions.why: Apologise for her experience without blaming anyone or promising what you cannot give, and say what happens next. Blaming a co-worker or the client, or promising freebies, causes more trouble.

questions.q: Mrs Grant has a blister on one leg. What is the most important action?
o: Put a cream from the salon shelf on the blister to soothe it and keep it clean
Tell her blisters are common after waxing and will go down within a day
Advise her to see a doctor, give first aid if trained, and report it
Wait to see how the leg looks tomorrow before deciding what to do about it
questions.why: A blister may be a burn, so treat it as a health matter first: care, advice to see a doctor and a report. Using a cream, reassuring her or waiting could make it worse.

questions.q: Why should the complaint be written on the salon's complaint record?
o: It lets the salon show the record to other clients as proof of its honesty and care
It shows what happened and what was agreed, so the team can improve
It allows the manager to decide which therapist should be dismissed after complaints
It stops the client from complaining a second time about the same treatment
questions.why: A record keeps the facts, shows who will act, and helps the team see causes, such as wax temperature, and prevent repeats. It is for improvement, not for punishment.

questions.q: Alecia hands Mrs Hall over with only 'She's all yours.' What should a proper handover include?
o: What was done, what is left and any concerns about her
Only the client's name and the time that she arrived at the salon today
Nothing more, because Brian can simply read the record card for the details
How pleasant or difficult the client has been so far during the visit
questions.why: A handover covers what was done, what is left, timing and concerns, so the client stays safe and the treatment is finished correctly. A vague message leads to mistakes.

questions.q: What is wrong with Brian telling his friend that Mrs Hall is pregnant?
o: He talked about a client while she was still in the salon, which is rude
He used the staff room for personal chat instead of keeping it for breaks
He should have told the whole team so that they could take extra care of her
He broke confidentiality by sharing her private health information
questions.why: Pregnancy is private health information. It may be shared only with the client's permission or with a person who needs it to treat her safely. Telling a friend, in front of a visitor, is a breach of confidentiality.

questions.q: Brian is angry about the untidy nail desk. What is the best first step?
o: Mention it to the next client to see what she thinks should be done about it
Leave an unsigned note on the desk so that Tasha knows how he feels
Calm down, then speak to Tasha in private using an 'I' statement
Say nothing, and tidy it himself every day so that there is no argument
questions.why: A calm, private 'I' statement deals with the problem without blaming her. Gossip, notes and silent resentment do not solve it. If talking fails, he can go to the supervisor.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann has an idea about confirming bookings by WhatsApp. What should she do at the meeting?
o: Keep quiet, because she is the most junior therapist in the room
Wait for the booking item, then offer the idea briefly
Interrupt Mrs Lyn at once so that she does not forget the idea
Tell the others after the meeting so that nobody can disagree with it
questions.why: A useful idea should be offered when it fits an agenda item, in turn and briefly. Staying silent wastes it, and interrupting is discourteous.
